evals.prompt: I run the platform team at Freightwise - we do shipment tracking APIs for 3PLs and freight brokers. We push about 4M webhooks a month, and our delivery worker already writes an attempts table with the HTTP response code and the timeout reason for every attempt, but it's internal-only, nobody outside engineering can see it. Support is burning roughly 15 hours a week on integration tickets. Leadership just approved 6 engineering weeks starting next month to build a developer-facing dashboard. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: A build order that starts from a classification of the recent support tickets, separates the three log surfaces, and recommends exposing the delivery-attempt data Freightwise already records as the first rung rather than building everything at once.
expectations: Recommends classifying the most recent integration support tickets by failure class (request not found, webhook never arrived, auth or credential failure, rate-limit confusion, silent data mismatch) before choosing what to build
Names the request log, the event log, and the webhook delivery-attempt log as three distinct surfaces rather than one combined dashboard
States that the delivery-attempt log answers 'did you tell me about it', the request log answers 'did my call work', and the event log answers 'what did it change'
Recommends exposing the existing delivery-attempt data as the first surface, on the grounds that it is already recorded and the remaining work is mostly access control and interface
Does not recommend building all three surfaces simultaneously inside the six-week window
States that a delivery-attempt row must carry the actual failure reason (timeout, connection refused, TLS failure, or a specific non-2xx status) rather than a generic 'delivery failed'
Lists the fields a delivery-attempt row carries, including event ID, destination endpoint, attempt number, attempt timestamp, and next scheduled retry time
Warns that a surface shipping only failure counts with no detail behind it converts a silent failure into a support ticket rather than into a fix
Asks or establishes what an integrator can see today without contacting Freightwise, as the audit baseline
Asks whether request and response bodies carry PII, secrets, or another tenant's data, and who signs off on exposing them to a third party
Asks whether this is a one-off fix after a bad support quarter or a compounding surface Freightwise will run for years, and ties that answer to which rung it recommends
Requires the dashboard to display the same identifiers Freightwise returns to integrators rather than internal primary keys

evals.prompt: Palmate is a B2B billing API. We return an X-Palmate-Request-Id header on 4xx and 5xx responses. Partners quote it in tickets and our support team tells me that roughly half the time the answer is 'that ID isn't in anything I can search'. Our edge assigns the ID, and then each internal service generates its own one for its own logs. We also call an external tax engine and a card processor on most requests. Fix this properly.
evals.expected_output: A correlation-identifier design that echoes one unchanged ID on every response, makes it resolvable in a surface the integrator can reach, and propagates it downstream and across retries.
expectations: Identifies that the ID is echoed only on failures, and requires echoing it on every response including 2xx, because a call that returned 200 and did the wrong thing is a real ticket class with no error body to carry the ID
Identifies per-service regeneration as a defect and requires one identifier to survive unchanged from the edge through every internal hop
States that echoing the header without an external surface that resolves it leaves integrators quoting a string nobody outside Palmate can look up
Recommends making the identifier searchable in a developer-facing log the integrator can reach themselves, and pairs that with the header rather than treating either rung as sufficient alone
Distinguishes a request ID, which identifies one HTTP call and its response, from a correlation ID, which identifies a multi-call transaction spanning several request IDs
Recommends forwarding the same identifier to the tax engine and the card processor instead of generating new ones at those hops
Justifies promoting downstream propagation by pointing at Palmate's current inability to see into failures that came from a provider it calls
Requires Palmate's own internal retries to carry the original identifier rather than generating a fresh one per attempt
Recommends logging the identifier on both sides of every boundary: inbound at the edge and outbound at each downstream call
Recommends accepting and echoing a client-supplied identifier when one arrives rather than overwriting it
Specifies an opaque random value such as a UUIDv4 and rejects sequential or timestamp-derived identifiers because they leak volume or timing and collide under concurrency
Does not redesign the error response payload shape, or explicitly defers the question of whether the ID rides in the error body to a separate error-design scope
Recommends documenting the lookup path next to the error documentation rather than on a separate observability page

evals.prompt: Nooklet sends an email to the partner's technical contact every time one of their webhook deliveries fails. We have 340 partner apps. Six of our top ten partners have admitted they filter us into a folder they never open. Our VP wants to add severity levels and route the important ones to Slack instead. Most of our partners reconcile bookings weekly, but two of them are payment-adjacent and lose real money inside an hour when their integration breaks. What should the notification design actually be?
evals.expected_output: A notification design that removes per-failure alerting entirely, defaults to a per-integration digest, and promotes threshold alerting with a cooldown only for the two money-losing partners.
expectations: Rejects per-failure alerting on error volume as a design option outright rather than ranking it last, naming it as the alert-fatigue failure mode itself
Recommends a periodic per-integration digest as the default notification rung for the majority of Nooklet's partners
Recommends threshold alerting with a cooldown specifically for the two payment-adjacent partners, tying that promotion to their losing money within hours

Specifies a cooldown period during which the same integration cannot alert again, and explains that without it one ongoing incident produces a continuous stream until the recipient mutes the channel permanently
Advises deriving the cooldown length from Nooklet's own typical incident duration rather than copying a borrowed number
Treats integration state changes such as revoked credentials, a disabled integration, or a lapsed subscription as a separate immediate rung with no threshold and no cooldown
Requires a recovery notification when the rate returns to baseline, on the grounds that silence is not an all-clear
Requires every alert to name the top machine-readable error codes and to link directly into the log filtered to those failures
Requires a threshold alert to state whether a Nooklet release falls in the window, so the partner knows what the platform has already ruled out
Requires a threshold alert to state the earliest time the next alert for that integration can arrive
States that the digest and the threshold alert must not be routed to the same destination at the same cadence
Recommends tracking the share of alerts partners act on, and treats a sustained decline as the design failing rather than the partners failing
Specifies an escalation path naming where a repeated unacted-on alert goes and after what interval
Does not present adding severity levels to the existing per-failure emails as the fix

evals.prompt: Gridwell exposes an HR data API to payroll and benefits vendors. Our partner dashboard shows one number: 'error rate, last 24h'. We page ourselves when any partner crosses 5%. Last week a partner sat at 4.2% all week while 100% of one specific app's calls were failing, and we never noticed. We also don't tag requests by app at the edge - we can join back to the API key afterwards from the auth service logs. And our biggest partner scaled 8x last month and went red purely from throttling. Rebuild the aggregation.
evals.expected_output: A per-identity aggregation schema tagged at ingestion, split into separate 4xx/5xx/429 buckets, compared against each integration's own baseline across two detection windows, with deploy markers overlaid.
expectations: Requires tagging each request with the integration identity at ingestion, and rejects reconstructing the tag afterwards by joining auth-service logs
States that retrofitting the identity tag leaves the preceding history unqueryable per integration, which is exactly the period any investigation needs
Splits the error rate into at least three separately counted buckets: 4xx, 5xx, and 429
Explains that 429 is isolated because rate-limit rejection is neither party's defect, and that blending it makes a partner scaling successfully look identical to a partner whose code is broken
Attributes 4xx to the integrator's side and 5xx to Gridwell's side, and states that a blended number cannot say whose problem the errors are
Replaces the single 5% platform-wide threshold with a comparison of each integration against its own recent baseline
Explains that one global percentage is either noise for low-traffic integrations or blindness for high-traffic ones
Requires the aggregate row to carry a success count as the denominator alongside the error counts
Requires explicit window start and end on each aggregate rather than a floating rate
Requires the top machine-readable error codes per bucket in the aggregate
Overlays Gridwell's own deploy or release markers on the error-rate view, and requires checking a 5xx spike against that timeline before telling a partner anything
Specifies both a short detection window measured in minutes for sudden breaks and a long window of hours to a day for slow degradation, and states that a single window misses half the failure types
Recommends reading how errors are distributed rather than volume alone, distinguishing a clustered pattern (logic bug or bulk operation) from an evenly spread one (infrastructure)

evals.prompt: Kettleback partners keep asking for two things. First, a button to re-send webhook events their endpoint missed during their own maintenance windows. Second, a 'retry this call' button on failed POST /orders requests in our log viewer. We already retry webhooks automatically 6 times over 12 hours. One partner wants to bulk re-send everything that failed during a 4-hour outage on their side, which is about 90,000 events. Design both features.
evals.expected_output: Event replay designed with a stable event ID, a bounded published window, rate-controlled bulk scope, and independence from the automatic retry schedule - plus a refusal to build synchronous request replay.
expectations: Refuses to build a replay button that re-issues the failed POST /orders request on the integrator's behalf, and explains that re-issuing it creates side effects nobody authorised
Recommends instead surfacing the full request detail so the integrator's own client re-issues the call
Approves event replay for the webhook case and ties the promotion to partners losing events during their own downtime, which is Kettleback's stated situation
Requires the replayed delivery to carry the same event ID as the original so the consumer can deduplicate
States that without a stable event ID replay converts a missed event into a duplicated side effect, a worse failure than the one it fixed
Requires manual replay to run independently of Kettleback's automatic six-attempt retry schedule, without cancelling or resetting it
Warns that a manual resend issued while automatic retries are still scheduled can produce a duplicate delivery, and addresses that specific overlap
Defines a bounded window measured from event creation beyond which replay is not offered, and requires publishing it
Requires rate control on the 90,000-event bulk replay, and states that an unthrottled bulk replay turns the partner's recovery into Kettleback's next incident
Decides the replay scope explicitly among per-event, per-endpoint, and per-time-range rather than leaving it implicit
Identifies replay as the highest-effort item on the visibility menu rather than a quick win
Does not recommend having a manual resend cancel or supersede the in-flight automatic retries

evals.prompt: Tuliphase has a per-customer dashboard where any admin of that customer's account can see every API call their integrations made - full request log, 30 days, searchable, with bodies. We're genuinely proud of it. We have 22 ISV partners whose apps are installed across roughly 6,000 of our customers. Every single time one of those apps breaks, the ISV finds out from their own customers, not from us. Our head of partnerships thinks we need to promote the dashboard harder. Diagnose it.
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the per-account dashboard is structurally wrong for fleet partners, requiring cross-install aggregation keyed on the app ID plus push notification, and a separate access-model fix.
expectations: States the problem is structural rather than a matter of awareness, and rejects promoting the existing dashboard as the fix
Explains that a per-account dashboard cannot serve an ISV whose app is installed across thousands of accounts, because nobody watches thousands of dashboards
Requires cross-install aggregation keyed on the app or client ID, spanning every install of one ISV's app, as the missing surface
Requires push notification to the ISV rather than relying on them to come and look

Identifies the access model as a distinct gap: the ISV engineer who maintains the integration is typically not a user of the customer's account and therefore cannot open the per-account dashboard at all
Distinguishes the single-account integrator segment from the ISV-fleet segment, and states that a surface designed for the first does not finish the job for the second
Recommends an installs-affected against installs-total measure per ISV app, and reads that ratio as the diagnosis
Interprets a high installs-affected ratio as a partner-side release and a low one as configuration trouble at a few customers
Does not conclude that Tuliphase's existing per-account request log was the wrong thing to have built
Recommends deciding explicitly who can read each surface: the account owner, any user of the account, and the partner engineer outside the account
Scopes the notification audience to the 22 ISVs rather than to the individual customer accounts

evals.prompt: Verandaq's integration health board was all green for eleven days. Then a partner emailed asking why none of their stock syncs had landed since the 3rd. Their scheduler had died on the 3rd and they simply stopped calling us - zero requests, zero errors, board stayed green the whole time. Our SRE lead wants to add a 'no traffic' alert that fires when any integration drops below 10 calls per hour. What's the right design here?
evals.expected_output: A volume-drop signal designed as its own item, baselined per integration rather than against a global floor, surfaced in the fleet view and pushed to the partner.
expectations: Rejects a single platform-wide floor of ten calls per hour, and explains that integrations differ in traffic shape by orders of magnitude
Requires comparing each integration's call volume against that integration's own recent baseline instead of a fixed number
States explicitly that an absence of calls produces no errors and therefore appears nowhere in an error log or error-rate view
Treats the volume-drop signal as its own design item rather than a side effect of the error logging already in place
Requires silent integrations to appear in the provider-side fleet view alongside the erroring ones
Notes that silent failures are frequently the most expensive class precisely because neither side has noticed
Recommends notifying the partner about the drop rather than waiting for them to ask
Places the volume-drop signal outside the 4xx, 5xx and 429 status-code buckets rather than inside them
Uses a long enough comparison window that a single quiet interval does not fire the signal
Records this failure class as its own row in the visibility audit alongside the error classes
Does not claim that better error alerting or a lower error threshold would have caught this

evals.prompt: Sablecrest wants two things built. An internal partner error leaderboard: every partner sorted by total errors in the last 24 hours, descending, top 20 on a TV in the partner team's area. And a 0-100 Integration Health Score shown to each partner in their portal, which we'll use to decide who keeps Premier tier next year. Write the spec.
evals.expected_output: A fleet view ranked by blast radius with contact ownership and a separate regression queue, plus hard constraints on publishing any partner-facing score that drives commercial tiering.
expectations: Rejects sorting the fleet view by raw error count and requires ranking by blast radius instead
Explains that a partner app failing across many installs outranks a single account throwing more absolute errors, because one conversation fixes many problems
Requires installs affected against installs total per partner app as a dimension of the view
Requires a dominant status-code bucket per row so the queue separates the partner's payloads from Sablecrest's own failures from quota rejection
Requires a named contact owner on each row, on the grounds that a ranked list with no contact becomes a report nobody acts on
Requires first-seen timestamps aligned against both Sablecrest's release timeline and, where known, the partner's
Separates integrations broken since Sablecrest's own deploy into a distinct view or tab from the partner-outreach queue, and identifies the first as Sablecrest's own regression queue
Requires silent integrations whose call volume dropped toward zero to appear in the view
Warns against publishing a per-partner reliability number Sablecrest cannot defend line by line, because it will be quoted back in commercial conversations
Requires the inputs behind any partner-facing score to be inspectable by that partner: error counts, install coverage, and the windows used
Requires a documented recomputation and dispute process before the score can affect Premier tier, rather than after the first complaint
Rules out showing a partner where they rank against named competitors
States that volume alone is not health, and that a large partner at a stable low error rate is healthier than a small partner at a high one
Requires Sablecrest to set and defend its own weights rather than borrowing another product's weighting

evals.prompt: Our new platform director came from an SRE background. She wants each of our 40 integration partners at Marrowpoint to get a 99.9% availability SLO with a monthly error budget, published in the partner portal, and she wants us to explain to partners that because they depend on us plus two other vendors, their achievable availability is capped below 99.7%. She's asked me to write the spec this week. Sanity-check it before I do.
evals.expected_output: A separation of which parts of SRE error-budget practice transfer to a provider-side integration view and which do not, with a refusal to publish a per-partner SLO derived from integration health.
expectations: States that the published error-budget and SLO literature is written consumer-side, for a team measuring its own dependence on someone else's API, and does not transfer wholesale to a provider publishing numbers for partners
Rejects presenting the multi-vendor multiplicative availability argument to Marrowpoint's partners, because that arithmetic describes the consumer's position rather than Marrowpoint's
Warns that an integration measurement includes the partner's own code and their customers' configuration, so committing to a number derived from it is a promise Marrowpoint only partly controls
Routes formal SLA and uptime publication to a separate status-and-incident-communication scope rather than deriving it from the integration health view
Keeps per-integration and per-endpoint granularity as a part that does transfer, against a single blended platform number
Keeps multi-window burn-rate detection as a part that does transfer: a long window confirming the problem is sustained plus a short window confirming it is still active
States that nothing in the published record establishes what a provider-side integration SLO should contain
Advises against publishing any per-partner number before Marrowpoint can defend how it is computed
Frames the goal of being the trustworthy real-time source of integration health as a design intent rather than an industry standard to cite to partners
Does not simply approve writing the 99.9% per-partner SLO spec as requested
Recommends an internal prioritisation view first, and distinguishes it from a partner-facing published grade as two different products with different obligations
Notes that a partner-facing number becomes a contract the moment partners start optimising against it

evals.prompt: Clovermast processes medical claims. Legal has given us a written answer: request and response bodies contain PHI and must never be visible outside our tenancy boundary, no exceptions, not negotiable. Meanwhile about 70% of our support pile is 'my call failed and I don't know why' on synchronous POSTs. Our current log viewer shows timestamp, method, path, and status code, and nothing else. Design what we can actually ship.
evals.expected_output: A metadata-only request log treated as the ceiling rather than a compromise, with error codes, identifiers and identity added, and structural tenant isolation plus unconditional credential stripping.
expectations: Removes payload-level logging from the option set entirely rather than ranking it lower or proposing a masked version of it
States that metadata-only logging is the ceiling in Clovermast's case rather than a compromise position
Adds a machine-readable error code to every row, and states that a bare 400 tells the integrator nothing their own client did not already know
Adds a request ID to every row, copy-pasteable and searchable by the integrator
Adds the integration identity and the account it acted on to every row
Adds latency to the row
Requires an error detail or reason field naming which field or condition failed, constructed without echoing the payload itself
Requires credentials, tokens and signing secrets to be stripped unconditionally rather than partially masked, because a prefix plus a length is often enough to attack
Requires any withheld field to be visibly marked as withheld so the integrator can tell it was suppressed rather than absent
Requires tenant isolation to be enforced structurally rather than by an application-code filter on account ID
Treats the redaction rule set as a published contract once integrators build against it, noting that loosening it later is a privacy incident and tightening it later breaks their tooling
Prioritises the synchronous request log over the other surfaces on the strength of the 70% synchronous share of the support pile
Does not propose negotiating with legal or seeking an exception as the path forward

evals.prompt: Plumridge is a payroll API. Two problems. First, we keep integration logs for 24 hours to keep storage costs down, but our customers reconcile payroll monthly. Second, about 60% of the people building against us aren't engineers - they're ops staff wiring us into no-code automation tools, and their tickets literally say 'it's not working'. Our log viewer today shows raw JSON request and response pairs plus HTTP status codes. What do we change?
evals.expected_output: A retention window sized to the monthly reconciliation cycle and published, plus a separate plain-language failure surface for the non-engineer segment that does not replace the detailed one.
expectations: States that a 24-hour retention window against monthly reconciliation guarantees the evidence expires before the investigation starts
Requires the retention window to exceed the time it realistically takes a Plumridge customer to notice a failure, and sizes it against the monthly cycle
Requires the retention window to be published rather than discovered during an incident
Identifies the no-code and non-engineer builders as a distinct audience segment with different needs from engineers integrating directly
Recommends a plain-language failure list scoped to that builder's own flow rather than raw JSON request and response pairs
Requires a 'what to do about it' line next to each failure entry for that segment
States that the detail useful to an engineering integrator reads as noise to the no-code segment
Keeps the detailed surface for the engineering segment rather than replacing it wholesale with the simplified one
Recommends classifying Plumridge's 'it's not working' tickets by failure class to decide which surface to build first
Treats the retention change and the audience change as two separate items rather than one
Names log retention shorter than time-to-notice as a failure mode that generates tickets regardless of how good the log row is
